doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: First recordings of the band in March 1933, with Carter vocals
summary: Carter dislikes talk of his early vocals, and says recording was another gig that brought a check.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: While we’re on those recordings, maybe we can backtrack a little to the first . . . those were in October, but in April you had done some recording with your band, actually the first other than that mysterious 1932 Tell All Your Daydreams anomaly, I guess we might call it, because it’s not typical, I think, of what you would do.
No. Well, I don’t remember that at all, really.
Right. It’s clear that you’re on it, but it’s not clear what . . . about it or . . .
You can’t understand why.
Yeah, okay. [laughter] Well, I was going to put it more diplomatically, but, well, strange things happen.
Well, yeah.

Anyway, your own band got to record in a much more favorable light in March, although the March one is sort of a strange date there, too. There are a lot of vocals, and this is before Teddy Wilson. This is with Nicholas Rodriguez on piano, but the band is pretty much intact otherwise. You have Chu Berry and Sid Catlett. Just to refresh your memory, there’s Swing It, Synthetic Love, Spike Hughes’ composition, Six Bell Stampede, and Love, You’re Not the One for Me. Those have Benny Carter vocals.
I was hoping that you wouldn’t bring that up.
[laughs] Well, I won’t make . . .
Knowing full well I could rely on your doing so.
Well, I won’t play them for you, if that’s any consolation.
Play them if you like. I won’t listen. [laughter]

But I’m just wondering, you know, this band had been rehearsing for some time, although . . . yeah, for about a year almost at this point, and this is your first opportunity to record them. I think this was another John Hammond production for . . .
I think . . . oh yes, surely.
. . . for English Columbia.
That’s right.
But the repertoire seems a little strange, to do all these vocals, which I’m not sure whether you were . . . you were not then known as a vocalist, I don’t think.
No, and I’m still not.
Well, I would say your vocal talents have come much more to the fore in recent years. But do you remember anything about how these particular pieces were done on that first date, and why?
No, I don’t, to answer both of your questions, how and why. Well, why was, of course, we were . . . part of it, it was another gig.
Right.
You know, for every recording that we did, we got a check.
Sure. Was there a feeling that perhaps they might be more commercially acceptable or commercially viable?
Oh, of course. That always entered into it at that time.
With vocals.
Yes.
And with these sort of, you know . . .
Yes, that might have been it.
